meta: Utagawa Toyoharu's 1767 perspective print of Sanjūsangendō, the long Buddhist hall in Fukagawa where archers shot along the veranda.
about: A long wooden hall runs back in steep perspective beside a crowded lane with pine trees, market stalls and figures in kimono. It is Sanjūsangendō, a Buddhist temple that houses 1001 statues of Kannon, a Buddhist goddess. At one end an archer kneels and shoots an arrow into the bull's-eye of a target at the far end of the building. A judge's stand waits nearby. Utagawa Toyoharu made the print in 1767.

meta: Utamaro II's 1806 print of Daikoku, the god of good fortune, with a boy holding a toy boat and a rat.
about: Daikoku, one of the seven lucky gods of Japan, sits on baskets with his mallet in his right hand. A young boy sits in front of him and holds up a toy boat with a rat sitting on it. Utamaro II made the print in 1806. The title adds Chinese children to the scene.

meta: Utagawa Hiroshige's 1857 night view of Tsukuda island from Eitai bridge, with a half moon over the water.
about: The view is taken from water level, with a pillar of Eitai bridge on the left and the helm of a passing boat on the right. Ships lie at anchor nearby, and Tsukuda island is the low shape in the background. A half moon hangs in the sky above, with a few scattered stars. Small boats carry glowing lanterns across the rippling water. Utagawa Hiroshige made the print in 1857.

meta: Utagawa Kuniyasu's 1815 print of act three of the Chūshingura, with Kampei raising his sword at the entrance to a foot-bridge.
about: At the entrance to a foot-bridge, a man named Kampei holds his sword over his head, poised to strike. Okaru, a woman in a patterned kimono and red collar, stands next to him. On the ground lies a man who may be one of the ruffians working for Moronō. Utagawa Kuniyasu made the print in 1815 for act three of the Chūshingura. A red wooden bridge crosses behind them.

meta: Utagawa Kuniyasu's 1815 print of act six of the Chūshingura, in which Osai arrives by palanquin to pay for Okaru.
about: Osai, who owns a brothel, arrives in a palanquin with porters at the front and back. She has come to Yoichibei's cottage to make the final payment for Okaru, his daughter. Kampei confronts her. He is returning from a night of hunting, during which he accidentally shot and killed the outlaw Sadakurō, who had just killed and robbed Yoichibei. Utagawa Kuniyasu made the print in 1815. Rice paddies and distant hills fill the background.

meta: Torii Kiyonaga's 1781 print of the young calligrapher Gyokkashi Eimo with her writing teacher at a low table.
about: Gyokkashi Eimo, a young girl with a talent for calligraphy, sits at a low table with her writing instructor, a young woman in a striped kimono. Fans and brushes hang in the background. More fans lie on the floor with sheets of paper. Torii Kiyonaga made the print in 1781. Look at the hanging slips, which carry inscriptions.

meta: Okumura Masanobu's 1711 woodcut parody of the Chinese sage Tieqiao, with a small man rising on a puff of air.
about: One woman holds her hands over a man's eyes and blows a puff of air, and a small male figure rises on it. A second woman waves to the figure and seems to be offering him a small package. Okumura Masanobu made the print in 1711 as a parody of the Chinese sage Tieqiao. It is printed in black and white. The small figure balances on a rope in the upper left.

meta: Utagawa Kunisada's 1847 kabuki triptych of three actors in costume with others dressed as a lion, a tiger and an elephant.
about: A night scene lit by a lantern fills three sheets, taken from a kabuki play. On the left the actor Hachiman Tarō Yoshiie stands with a parasol beside an unidentified actor dressed as a lion. In the centre is Abe no Sadato with another unidentified actor dressed as a tiger. On the right the actress Sadato no Tsuma, Abe no Sadato's wife, appears with a third unidentified actor in an elephant costume. Utagawa Kunisada made the triptych in 1847.
dimensions: 34.9 x 73.6 cm (whole image), 34.9 x 24.5 cm (left panel), 34.9 x 24.5 cm (center panel), 34.9 x 24.6 cm

meta: J. E. H. MacDonald's 1919 poster for the Canadian National Exhibition in Toronto, with a woman on horseback standing for Canada.
about: A woman on a horse, representing Canada, holds the British flag. Next to her stands a Canadian soldier, and an airplane flies overhead. Behind them lie the exhibition grounds. Various other war-related items appear in the picture. J. E. H. MacDonald made the lithograph in 1919 to advertise the Canadian National Exhibition. Bold lettering announces the event below the picture.

meta: A 1916 German poster announcing the war exhibition in Hamburg, organised by the Red Cross.
about: Black and red curved forms sweep across a beige ground above a dense block of sans-serif text. The poster may show a stylized German flag. It announces a war exhibition sponsored by the Central Committee of the Association of the German Red Cross and the Hamburg Regional Association of the Red Cross. The text gives the place, the dates and the entrance fee. The exhibition was held at the Ernst Merckhalle in the Zoological Garden. The sheet dates from 1916.

meta: George Fess's play Day Is Darkness on a 1939 Federal Theatre Project poster from Boyle Heights, California.
about: A man stands with his arms spread before a ring of fire. The poster advertises the Federal Theatre Project's production of Day Is Darkness at the Ocean Park Municipal Auditorium in Boyle Heights, California. The title calls it a famous anti-Nazi play in three acts by George Fess, directed by Adolph Freeman. Some of the text is in Yiddish. The silkscreen poster dates from 1939. Performance details are printed in black on cream.

meta: A 1936 Federal Theatre Yiddish Unit poster for David Pinski's comedy The Tailor Becomes a Storekeeper in Chicago.
about: A man and a sewing machine share the design of this poster for The Tailor Becomes a Storekeeper. The Federal Theatre Yiddish Unit presented the comedy by David Pinski, with music, at the Great Northern Theatre on West Jackson near State Street in Chicago. Some of the text is in Yiddish. The silkscreen dates from 1936. It uses bold red, black and cream lettering.

meta: A 1936 Federal Art Project poster for an exhibition from the Index of American Design in Boston, with a weather vane in the shape of a Native American.
about: A figure in a feathered headdress and beaded necklace draws a bow and arrow against a tan and blue geometric ground. It is a weather vane in the shape of a Native American. The poster announces an exhibition of art work from the Index of American Design. The Federal Art Project held it at the Federal Art Gallery, 50 Beacon Street, in Boston. Russell W. West made the silkscreen in 1936.

meta: A 1936 poster for the Detroit Federal Theatre's production of Sinclair Lewis's It Can't Happen Here at the Lafayette Theatre.
about: A stylized Adolf Hitler carrying a rifle stands behind a map of the United States, next to a fist in a raised-arm salute. The poster advertises It Can't Happen Here by Sinclair Lewis. The Detroit Federal Theatre Project, a unit of the Michigan Works Progress Administration, presented the play at the Lafayette Theatre. The silkscreen dates from 1936.

meta: Maurice Merlin's 1936 silkscreen poster for Michigan Art Month, urging people to buy the work of Michigan artists.
about: A nude sculpture of a woman stands inside an open picture frame on a yellow tiled floor, with a palette and pottery nearby. The poster announces Michigan Art Month, held from 1 November to 1 December. It encourages citizens to learn about the art work of Michigan artists and to buy it. Local sales exhibitions were to be found near each viewer. Maurice Merlin made it in 1936.

meta: A 1936 Federal Theatre Project poster for The Tailor Becomes a Storekeeper at Daly's Theatre in New York.
about: A hand holds a fish that is being cut in half with scissors. A needle with a looping thread and some musical notes complete the design. The poster is for the Federal Theatre Project's production of The Tailor Becomes a Storekeeper by David Pinski, called a grotesque comedy. It played at Daly's Theatre, on 63rd Street east of Broadway in New York City. The silkscreen dates from 1936.

meta: A 1936 poster for two chamber operas, The Romance of Robot and La Serva Padrona, put on by the Federal Music Project in New York.
about: Blue, black, cream and yellow blocks form a geometric design. The poster advertises two chamber operas from the Federal Music Project of New York City. One is The Romance of Robot, a romantic satire by Frederic Hart and Tillman Breiseth. The other is La Serva Padrona, a comic interlude by Pergolesi. Felix Brentano devised and directed the staging, with Paul Vellucci as music director and Felicia Sorel as choreographer. Performances were at the W.P.A. Theatre of Music, 254 West 54th Street.

meta: A 1990 facsimile of the Federal Theatre poster for Theodore Ward's drama Big White Fog, staged by Kay Ewing.
about: A man is trapped in a fog that stretches from a hut in Africa to a big city, where a dark skyscraper rises through stylized clouds. This is a facsimile of a poster for the Federal Theatre Project's production of Big White Fog by Theodore Ward. The International House Theatre, at 1414 East 59th Street, sponsored it. Kay Ewing staged the play. The facsimile is dated 1990.

meta: A 1937 Federal Theatre poster for Jean Bart's drama The Squall in Colton, California.
about: A woman in a red blouse and dark patterned skirt stands in front of a yellow arched door. She is a full-length portrait of a Spanish woman. The poster advertises The Squall, Jean Bart's drama of romantic Spain, as a Federal Theatre Road Attraction of the W.P.A. It ran at the Federal Theatre in Colton, California, from 27 April to 2 May. The silkscreen dates from 1937.

meta: A 1938 Hollywood Playhouse poster for Clemence Dane's play Will Shakespeare, a Federal Theatre Project production.
about: A half-timbered cottage with a green roof stands beside an ornate wrought iron bracket that holds a wooden sign reading Will. The poster shows part of a building, possibly the Globe Theatre. It advertises the Federal Theatre Project's presentation of Will Shakespeare by Clemence Dane, subtitled his life and loves. The play was staged at the Hollywood Playhouse, at Vine and Hollywood Boulevard in Los Angeles. The silkscreen dates from 1938.

meta: A 1936 Federal Theatre poster for Bernard Shaw's Devil's Disciple in New Orleans, with a cartoon head wearing a halo.
about: A cartoon drawing of a head in profile wears a red cravat and has a halo above it. The poster advertises the Federal Theatre Project's presentation of Devil's Disciple by Bernard Shaw. It ran from 12 to 17 October at the Federal Theatre Playhouse, at Tulane and Miro in New Orleans, Louisiana. The poster is red and green silkscreen from 1936.

meta: Anthony Velonis's 1936 WPA poster arguing that better housing could cut infant mortality in the slums.
about: A planned housing community fills the foreground, and behind it a crossed-out telescopic view shows a block of tenements. The poster argues that better housing is the solution to high rates of infant mortality in the slums. A circular inset shows a woman with a pram beside tenement buildings. The sheet names the New York City Housing Authority, under Mayor Fiorello La Guardia and Commissioner Langdon W. Post. Anthony Velonis made the silkscreen in 1936.

meta: Utagawa Hiroshige's 1833 print of Ishiyakushi, a station on the Tōkaidō Road, with travelers entering the village.
about: Three travelers, one of them on horseback, enter a village at the Ishiyakushi station on the Tōkaidō Road. Two porters with a shoulder pole walk on a berm between two fields, where haystacks stand and laborers work. The village lies in the background beneath a blue-green mountain with layered ridges. Utagawa Hiroshige made the print in 1833. Pale mist hangs on the slopes.

meta: Katsushika Hokusai's 1804 print of Odawara, with a woman beside a large trunk and a porter holding a small box.
about: A woman stands next to a large trunk, possibly pondering an offer from the other traveler or porter sitting beside it. He holds up a small box in his raised left hand. A large building, perhaps a castle or temple, stands in the background on the left. Katsushika Hokusai made the print in 1804. Look for the calligraphy marked on the trunk.

meta: Katsushika Hokusai's 1804 print of Nissaka, where a street performer plays miniature drums on a spread cloth.
about: A man stands on a large square of cloth spread on the ground, playing miniature drums that hang at his waist. He wears a miniature torii over his shoulders. Behind him another man sits on the cloth and plays drums too. Coins lie scattered across it. Katsushika Hokusai made the print in 1804.

meta: Katsushika Hokusai's 1832 print of the weir at Senju in Musashi Province, with Mount Fuji far behind.
about: Two people fish at the weir at Senju in the province of Musashi. A man leads a horse that carries rice seedlings to be planted in the distant paddies, and Mount Fuji rises in the background. Katsushika Hokusai made the print in 1832. A pencil inscription on the card kept with the item gave the library's cataloguers the location.

meta: A 1936 Federal Theatre Project poster for George Bernard Shaw's comedy Captain Brassbound's Conversion at the Hollywood Playhouse.
about: A stylized profile portrait of a bearded man stands beside large display lettering. The man is Bernard Shaw, whose three-act comedy Captain Brassbound's Conversion is advertised. The Federal Theatre Project presented it at the Hollywood Playhouse, on Vine Street near Hollywood Boulevard in Los Angeles. The poster also lists nightly performances and ticket prices. Silkscreen, 1936.

meta: Utagawa Kuniyoshi's 1844 print of the warrior Gorō Mitsutoki, bristling with arrows, reporting aboard a Taira ship at Dannoura.
about: Mitsutoki wears protective padded armor with several arrows sticking out of it. He prostrates himself on board a Taira ship, reporting to Tomomori, Emperor Antoku and others during the battle of Dannoura. His expression is fierce. Blue waves crash beyond the railing on the wooden deck. Utagawa Kuniyoshi made the print in 1844.

meta: Utagawa Kuniyasu's 1815 print of act one of the Chūshingura, where Moronō's love letter to Kaoyo leads to a drawn sword.
about: Kaoyo stands on the left, the wife of Enya, who is also known as Asano Naganori. She has received a love letter from Moronō, also called Kira Yoshinaka, and he stands on the right. Between them, Wakasanosuke is about to draw his sword. Utagawa Kuniyasu made this print in 1815. A wall of hexagonal stones runs behind the three figures.

meta: Richard Halls's 1936 poster for the Federal WPA Variety Theatre's vaudeville show of nine acts.
about: A cheerful performer in a top hat sings, holding a cane, while stylized monkeys play around him. The poster advertises a Federal Theatre Project vaudeville show of nine big acts. Among them are Tumble In, Emil Jarrow, a Dance Parade Review and the Laing Brothers. Richard Halls made the silkscreen in 1936.

meta: Archie Gunn's 1895 poster for The Love Adventures of Al-Mansur, a book in the Rococo Series edited by Archibald Clavering Gunter.
about: A man in a red doublet, cape and pointed shoes opens a large bag labelled The Rococo Series in front of a woman in a white gown with black bows. She looks inside. The poster advertises The Love Adventures of Al-Mansur, a book published in 1895 and edited by Archibald Clavering Gunter. Archie Gunn drew it in red and black on a yellow ground. A line at the foot says the book is now ready and for sale here.

meta: Utagawa Hiroshige's 1855 bird's-eye view of the river at Kawasaki, a station on the Tōkaidō Road, with Mount Fuji beyond.
about: A bird's-eye view looks down on the river at Kawasaki, the station on the Tōkaidō Road. A sailboat crosses the water and a man poles a raft. A cluster of buildings stands at the end of a bridge. Snow-capped Mount Fuji rises in the background above layered hills. Utagawa Hiroshige made the print in 1855.

meta: Utagawa Hiroshige's 1855 print of Kanbara, the sixteenth station on the Tōkaidō Road, with pilgrims climbing between two buildings.
about: A bird's-eye view shows Kanbara, the sixteenth station on the Tōkaidō Road. Pilgrims in straw hats walk up an incline between two buildings, one of which may be a teahouse. In the distance boats move on a river, and beyond it rise mountains, Mount Fuji among them. Utagawa Hiroshige made the print in 1855.

meta: Utagawa Hiroshige's 1857 print of the autumn moon over the Ishiyama-dera temple, with the Seta River bridge below.
about: A full moon hangs over Ishiyama-dera, the Buddhist temple, which is seen from above. A building sits on a bluff, a pagoda stands among pines, and a bridge crosses the Seta River. The Library of Congress notes that this is the same bridge that appears in Evening glow at Seta. Mountains fill the distance. Utagawa Hiroshige made the print in 1857. A poem in calligraphy and a red title card sit at the top.

meta: Utagawa Hiroshige's 1833 print of Totsuka, a station on the Tōkaidō Road, where travelers arrive at an inn.
about: Travelers reach an inn or teahouse at the Totsuka station on the Tōkaidō Road. One mounts or dismounts a horse, and another crosses a bridge. A hanging sign marks the wooden inn. Thatched roofs of the village houses show beyond it. Utagawa Hiroshige made the print in 1833. A stone milestone stands beside the road.

meta: Utagawa Hiroshige's 1833 print of Seki on the Tōkaidō Road, with travelers outside a shop selling hats and short kimonos.
about: Travelers gather outside a men's clothing shop that sells hats and short kimonos, at the Seki station on the Tōkaidō Road. Others stand at the entrance to a gated area. Some shops are closed, and their fabric curtains carry painted designs. White curtains with round blue crests hang at the inn. Utagawa Hiroshige made the print in 1833.

meta: Utagawa Hiroshige's 1848 print of two women on the road at Mishima, one carrying grain and one holding a parasol hung with ladles.
about: Two women walk side by side in patterned kimono. One carries a tray of rice or grain on her head. The other holds a parasol from which wooden cooking utensils hang. Mishima is the twelfth station on the Tōkaidō Road, and the Library of Congress marks the identification of the women with a question mark. Utagawa Hiroshige made the print in 1848.

meta: Utagawa Hiroshige's 1848 print of travelers passing under pine trees at Yoshiwara, with Mount Fuji on the left.
about: A line of travelers with hats and bundles passes through a stand of pine trees near the Yoshiwara station on the Tōkaidō Road. Two of the pines twist across the green field. A cluster of buildings stands in the background on the right, and Mount Fuji rises on the left. Utagawa Hiroshige made the print in 1848.

meta: Utagawa Hiroshige's 1844 print of the long wooden bridge at Okazaki on the Tōkaidō Road, seen from below.
about: A wooden bridge spans a broad river at the Okazaki station on the Tōkaidō Road, and the viewer looks up at it from below. A man on horseback crosses it. Boats ride on the river, boatmen pole flat craft beneath the trestles, and buildings crowd the near background. Mountains close the distance. Utagawa Hiroshige made the print in 1844.

meta: Honoré Daumier's The Beggars, painted around 1843, a row of figures in profile that passed from the artist's widow to Peter A.B. Widener.
about: A row of figures in profile stands against a dark, muted ground. Warm light falls on their faces and bare shoulders. Honoré Daumier painted The Beggars around 1843. It passed to his wife, Marie-Alexandrine, and then to the dealer Durand-Ruel in New York, who sold it in 1892 to Peter A.B. Widener. Widener later exchanged it back to the dealer Knoedler. After several Paris owners, Gaston Bernheim de Villers bought it at the Hôtel Drouot sale of 1912 for his private collection.

meta: Frederic Edwin Church's Tamaca Palms, painted in 1854 for the collector Abraham M. Cozzens, later in the Corcoran Gallery.
about: A tall snow-capped mountain rises above brown foothills and a calm tropical river. Slender palms and dense foliage frame the left foreground. Frederic Edwin Church painted it in 1854 for the New York collector Abraham M. Cozzens. Years later he wrote that it was the first South American picture he ever painted, an early effort. The estate sale of Cozzens listed it as The Andes. It was given to the Corcoran Gallery of Art in 1869 and came to the National Gallery of Art in 2014.
credit_line: Corcoran Collection (Gift of William Wilson Corcoran, 1869)

meta: Paul Cézanne's portrait of his father reading the newspaper L'Événement, bought by the National Gallery of Art in 1970.
about: An older man in a dark cap and jacket sits in a floral armchair, absorbed in a newspaper whose masthead is partly visible. A framed still life with green fruit hangs on the wall beside him. The man is Louis-Auguste Cézanne, the painter's father, and the paper is L'Événement. The picture was shown at the Salon of 1882. It passed from the dealer Ambroise Vollard to the collector Auguste Pellerin, then to his heirs, and in 1970 to the National Gallery of Art with funds from Paul Mellon.
credit_line: Collection of Mr. and Mrs. Paul Mellon

meta: Jan Luyken's design showing the execution by gunpowder of the Anabaptist Hendrik Eemkens in Utrecht in 1562.
about: Eemkens, an Anabaptist, is tied to a stake at left with gunpowder hung from his neck. At right an executioner uses a pitchfork to raise a bundle of burning hay, and lines radiating outward from Eemkens's body show the explosion. A priest and many other figures watch. The scene takes place in the city square of Utrecht. Jan Luyken made this brown ink and wash design as an illustration for T.J. van Bragt's martyrs' book Het bloedig tooneel.

meta: Jean-Louis Forain's Behind the Scenes, painted around 1880, a dancer in a pale tutu and a man half hidden in the dark.
about: A young woman in a pale tutu stands before a loose, flowering backdrop. A man in a top hat and evening coat stands half hidden in the dark at the edge of the scene. Jean-Louis Forain painted it around 1880. The collector Lessing J. Rosenwald probably acquired it in 1930 from the dealer Charles Sessler in Philadelphia. He gave it to the National Gallery of Art in 1943.

meta: Winslow Homer's Home, Sweet Home, painted around 1863, two Union soldiers in camp, with a long record of owners to 1997.
about: Two soldiers in dark blue uniforms and kepis occupy the foreground of a military camp. One stands with his hands on his hips, and the other sits on a crate, writing or reading. Canvas tents, hanging equipment and a small campfire fill the ground behind them. Winslow Homer painted it around 1863. The New York dealer Samuel Putnam Avery possibly owned it, and it was offered at a sale in 1867. A Christie's sale in 1997 is the last step in its recorded sales before the National Gallery of Art.

meta: Paul Gauguin's Still Life with Peonies, painted in 1884 and inscribed to a friend, Théodore Gad.
about: A dense bouquet of red and pink peonies stands in a dotted green-and-yellow vase on a patterned, draped tablecloth. The inscription at upper left is addressed to M. Théodore Gad, the artist's friend. The provenance, however, names a different first owner: M. Haslauer of Rouen, to whom Gauguin gave the picture. Haslauer's family may have kept it for decades. The New York dealer Carstairs sold it in 1957 to Paul Mellon, who gave it to the National Gallery of Art in 1995.
credit_line: Collection of Mr. and Mrs. Paul Mellon

meta: Lucas Cranach the Elder's A Prince of Saxony, painted around 1517, a boy in a flower wreath given to the National Gallery of Art in 1947.
about: A young boy with shoulder-length blond hair wears a wreath of small white and gold flowers. He stands against a dark background in a brown cloak over a red sleeve patterned with scrolling designs, with a lace-trimmed collar. Lucas Cranach the Elder painted him around 1517. The Munich dealer Julius Böhler and August Salomon of Dresden owned it jointly through Paul Cassirer in Berlin. Ralph Harman Booth and Mary Batterman Booth of Michigan bought it in 1925 and gave it to the museum in 1947.

meta: Eugène Delacroix's A Horse Hitched to a Post, painted around 1820, from the Haro family to Paul Mellon.
about: A reddish-brown horse stands in profile on sandy ground, its head turned toward a rope tied to a weathered wooden post. Loose, rapid brushwork and a dark, stormy sky frame the animal against a broad plain. Eugène Delacroix painted it around 1820. It appeared in the sale held after his death at the Hôtel Drouot in 1864. The collector Etienne-François Haro then owned it, and his son Henri, until a Haro family sale in Neuilly in 1934. Paul Mellon and his wife gave it to the National Gallery of Art in 1994.
credit_line: Collection of Mr. and Mrs. Paul Mellon

meta: George Catlin's The Female Eagle, Shawano, painted in 1830, which stayed in the artist's family until 1912.
about: A woman with dark hair pulled back and a braid over one shoulder wears layered beaded necklaces, a beaded earring and a white fur wrap over a red patterned garment. She is shown in three-quarter view. George Catlin painted her in 1830. It passed by descent to his three daughters. The American Museum of Natural History bought it from one of them in 1912, and Paul Mellon acquired it in 1959. He gave it to the National Gallery of Art in 1965.

meta: Utagawa Hiroshige's 1855 print of Okabe, the twenty-second station on the Tōkaidō Road, with pilgrims in a steep valley.
about: Pilgrims walk along the Tōkaidō Road through a steep valley at Okabe, the twenty-second station. A small thatched shelter stands in the middle distance, beside a winding road. A large mountain rises behind it, partly lost in mist. Utagawa Hiroshige made the print in 1855. The travelers wear traditional dress.

meta: Vincent van Gogh's Flower Beds in Holland, his first garden painting, made at The Hague in 1883 and later sold off as rubbish.
about: Rectangular plots of blue, yellow, pink and red hyacinths run toward thatched cottages and leafless trees. The low vantage point gives a panoramic view. Wikipedia calls it Van Gogh's first garden painting, made in his second year in The Hague in 1883. It probably stayed with his family. A carpenter in Breda who stored it sold it as rubbish in 1902. That year it was shown in Rotterdam as Tulip country, although the flowers are hyacinths. Paul Mellon later bought it and gave it to the National Gallery of Art, and today it hangs in Washington.
dimensions:
overall: 48.9 x 66 cm (19 1/4 x 26 in.)
framed: 71.1 x 88.9 x 8.3 cm (28 x 35 x 3 1/4 in.)
credit_line: Collection of Mr. and Mrs. Paul Mellon

meta: Hendrick Goltzius's The Fall of Man, dated 1616, with a record of owners that may reach back to a Delft sale in 1644.
about: A nude man and woman recline beneath a fruit-laden tree while Eve hands an apple to Adam. A serpent coils in the branches above, and a small cherub peers from the leaves. Hendrick Goltzius signed it with a monogram and the date 1616. The National Gallery of Art lists a possible early owner, Boudewijn de Man of Delft, whose sale in 1644 included a picture called Adam and Eve. In 1996 the museum bought it at Christie's in New York.

meta: Edgar Degas's 1855 portrait René de Gas, a boy against an olive-green ground, later owned by Paul Mellon.
about: A young boy with short dark hair turns slightly toward the viewer against an olive-green ground. He wears a dark jacket, a white collar and a dark bow tie, and his gaze is direct and serious. The first owner on record is René de Gas himself, the sitter named in the title. After him the painting passed to Roland Nepveu-de Gas. A Paris sale in 1964 brought it to Wildenstein, and Paul Mellon bought it in 1968 and gave it to the National Gallery of Art in 1995.
credit_line: Collection of Mr. and Mrs. Paul Mellon

meta: Hiroshige's ferry at Rokugo crossing the Tama River, the Kawasaki print in his Fifty-Three Stations of the Tokaido Road.
about: Five passengers and the man rowing the boat sail across the Tama River. On the shore at Kawasaki, merchants and others wait to board. At left a lone man in red stands on a large pile of bamboo. Behind the figures rise the tops of buildings and houses. Far in the background, Mount Fuji appears at the right, and streaks of red cloud surround its base. A pack horse stands on the shore. The print belongs to The Fifty-Three Stations of the Tokaido Road.

meta: Otto Wagner's 1850 watercolour of a Biedermeier salon in a residence of the Duke of Leuchtenberg.
about: Little furniture fills this large salon, which is in the Biedermeier style. A gilt bronze lyre clock sits on a blond wood secretary, flanked by classical busts. The upholstered banquette and matching wall covering were a device used by the architect Leo von Klenze, and before him by his mentor Schinkel. Mid-century porcelains stand on Empire consoles and are reflected in tall mirrors. A great porcelain stove at right is partly hidden by a needlepoint fire screen. The museum thinks one portrait on the centre wall probably shows Eugène de Beauharnais, son of Josephine.

meta: Katsukawa Shunsho's scroll of seven women carrying shoes and a deerskin ball, a possible play on the court game kemari.
about: Seven women in elaborate kimono stand on a wooden veranda beside a latticed screen and blossoming trees. They carry shoes and a deerskin ball, the equipment for kemari. In that game players form a circle and kick a ball back and forth without letting it fall, and it was played at the Japanese imperial court as early as the seventh century. Kemari was traditionally played by men. The museum suggests the scene may be mitate, a play on words or images popular in the Edo period.

meta: Thomas Gainsborough's portrait of Master John Heathcote, painted for his parents and kept by the family until 1913.
about: A young child in a white dress with a blue sash holds a small bunch of wildflowers and a black hat. Behind stretches an open woodland landscape with a distant hill. Thomas Gainsborough painted it for the sitter's parents, John and Lydia Heathcote of Conington Castle. It descended in the family to a great-grandson, who sold it in 1913 through the dealer Agnew to Duveen Brothers. Baron Michelham then owned it until his estate sale in 1926.
credit_line: Given in memory of Governor Alvan T. Fuller by The Fuller Foundation, Inc.

meta: Jean Honoré Fragonard's Diana and Endymion, a mythological scene that passed from Sir Richard Wallace to a chain of heirs and dealers.
about: A reclining goddess floats on a cloud at upper left and reaches toward a seated youth in red drapery. He rests beside a flock of sheep and a dozing dog. A cupid with a bundle of pink roses hovers between them. The painting belonged to Sir Richard Wallace by 1883. It then went by inheritance to his wife, to her adviser Sir John Murray Scott, and to his friend Lady Sackville. She sold it in 1913 to the dealer Jacques Seligmann, and the dealer Knoedler passed it on in 1922 to the singer John McCormack.

meta: John Constable's Wivenhoe Park, Essex, painted in 1816 for Major-General Francis Slater Rebow and bought by Peter A.B. Widener in 1906.
about: A broad lake lies framed by mature trees, with cattle grazing in the foreground. A red brick house sits on a rise in the distance. John Constable painted it in 1816 for Major-General Francis Slater Rebow, who owned the estate near Colchester. It stayed in the Rebow family for generations. In 1906 Peter A.B. Widener bought it from the dealer Leo Nardus, and in 1942 his heirs gave it to the National Gallery of Art.

meta: Maerten van Heemskerck's Rest on the Flight into Egypt, painted around 1530 and sold in 1930 as a work by Jan van Scorel.
about: A seated woman in a red dress and striped blue and pink drapery holds a nude infant who stands on her lap and reaches for her shoulder. A winding river valley with towers, a column and a distant town stretches behind them. The painting was once in the collection of Heinrich Wilhelm Campe of Leipzig, and later his grandson's. When the heirs sold it in Berlin in 1930, the auction catalogue gave it to Jan van Scorel. The Kress Foundation bought it in 1952 and gave it to the National Gallery of Art in 1961.

meta: William Hogarth's A Scene from The Beggar's Opera, a stage-like prison interior later bought by Paul Mellon.
about: A stone prison interior stands framed by blue and gold theatre drapery. A central figure in a red coat is flanked by kneeling women in pale gowns and men in dark coats, while spectators in period dress crowd the sides. William Hogarth painted the scene around 1728. A sale in 1885 may have included it under a vague description. By 1905 Francis Capel Cure of Badger Hall owned it, and it went to his nephew. Paul Mellon bought it in 1975 and gave it to the National Gallery of Art in 1983.

meta: Mary Cassatt's 1875 portrait of her nephew Eddy Cassatt, inscribed to him from Aunt Mary and given to the National Gallery of Art in 2015.
about: A young boy in a red velvet suit with a lace collar and cuffs stands beside a shaggy terrier. He holds a riding crop in front of a dark draped curtain. The words Eddy, from Aunt Mary are inscribed at lower left. Mary Cassatt painted the portrait in 1875. It belonged to the boy's father, her brother Alexander Johnston Cassatt, and then went to a granddaughter and a great-grandniece of the artist. It came to the museum in 2015.
credit_line: Gift from the Family of Col. Edward Buchanan Cassatt

meta: Edwin Austin Abbey's Who Is Sylvia?, painted between 1896 and 1899 and bought by William A. Clark in 1901.
about: A woman in a pale gown with red sleeves and a jeweled pendant stands at the centre of an interior with a carved column and a patterned rug. A man in black leans on a carved pedestal at right, and a musician in a red hood plays nearby. Edwin Austin Abbey took three years over it and reworked it in 1900. The collector William A. Clark bought it from the artist in 1901 and left it to the Corcoran Gallery of Art. The National Gallery of Art acquired it in 2014.

meta: Howard Pyle's painting of Charles Thomson telling George Washington at Mount Vernon that he had been elected president.
about: In a pale grey reception room with a round table on twisted legs, an older man in a brown coat leans toward a standing man in black with powdered hair. The painting by Howard Pyle shows Charles Thomson, Secretary of the Continental Congress, informing George Washington of his election to the presidency of the United States. The meeting took place on 14 April 1789 in the reception room of Washington's mansion at Mount Vernon in Virginia.

meta: A portrait of Mrs. George Collier, once thought to be by Joshua Reynolds and now given to a follower, with a nod to Catullus's Lesbia.
about: A woman in a white dress with a blue sash and a pink rose at her bodice turns her head down. A golden shawl lies over her shoulders. The painting was given to the Cleveland Museum in 1920 by the collector Jeptha H. Wade, who believed it was by Joshua Reynolds. After study, the museum gave it to a follower of Reynolds working in a similar style. It shows the wife of Captain George Collier, later an admiral. The painter compares her to Lesbia, the married woman who inspired the Roman poet Catullus and mourned her pet sparrow.

meta: Nicolaes Berchem's View of an Italian Port, painted in the early 1660s and once part of a Leiden collection sold for 100,000 florins.
about: Two riders on a white horse and a brown horse stand in the foreground, surrounded by cattle, goats, sheep and dogs on a sandy shore. Moored boats with furled sails lie beside a large ship with red pennants. Johan van Lanschot of Leiden owned the painting by 1753. It passed to his son-in-law and then to the grandson Diederik van Leyden, whose whole painting collection was sold for 100,000 florins to a consortium of three buyers. Part of it was auctioned in Paris in 1804.
credit_line: Gift of Robert H. and Clarice Smith, in Honor of the 50th Anniversary of the National Gallery of Art

meta: Heinrich Aldegrever's portrait of Bernard Knipperdolling, chief of the Anabaptists of Münster, with a laurel wreath around a sword.
about: Knipperdolling is shown at half length, his head in three-quarter view and turned to the right, with his hands clasped on the sill of a tablet below. At upper right, a laurel wreath encloses a hand gripping a sword. Aldegrever's monogram sits over the sitter's shoulder. A line in the margin calls it a true likeness of Bernt Knipperdollick, and the tablet carries a Latin verse with the date 1536.

meta: Gustave Courbet's The Stream, the Puits-Noir stream in the Loue valley, painted in 1855 and sold by Haro to Durand-Ruel in 1897.
about: A shadowed woodland stream runs between pale limestone cliffs, with slender trees and dense foliage overhanging the water. Rocks and mossy stones break the surface. Gustave Courbet dated it 1855. At the Laurent-Richard sale in Paris in 1878 it fetched 13,100 francs, catalogued as the Puits-Noir stream in the Loue valley. Later the Haro family owned it, and in 1897 the dealer Durand-Ruel sold it to Henry Osborn Havemeyer and his wife Louisine.
credit_line: Gift of Mr. and Mrs. P.H.B. Frelinghuysen in memory of her father and mother, Mr. and Mrs. H.O. Havemeyer

meta: William Adolphe Bouguereau's Bacchante on a Panther, one of six paintings made for Etienne Bartholony's house in Paris.
about: A nude woman with an ivy wreath rides a leaping spotted panther across an oval gold ground patterned with flowers, a pink drape billowing behind her. The picture belongs to a series of six paintings that decorated Etienne Bartholony's house in Paris. They imitate ancient Roman designs, with crisp cut-out forms against a gold background painted to look like mosaic. Its companion picture shows Arion, the Greek poet who escaped death on the back of a sea creature. They were shown at the Paris Salon in 1857.

meta: Claude Joseph Vernet's Morning, a misty harbour at dawn, probably one of four paintings ordered by Monsieur Journû of Bordeaux.
about: A misty harbour wakes at dawn. A round stone tower stands on the left, a campfire glows in the lower left corner, and fishermen work along the shore. The Art Institute of Chicago thinks Claude Joseph Vernet painted it as one of four pictures commissioned by Monsieur Journû of Bordeaux in 1759. It then descended in the Journu-Auber family until at least 1801. At the Hôtel Drouot in 1910 it was sold with its three companion pieces to Théodore Bonjean.
credit_line: Mr. and Mrs. Martin A. Ryerson Collection

meta: Carel Adolph Lion Cachet's 1874 painting of the head of a red-haired boy, given to the Rijksmuseum by the artist's son in 1968.
about: A boy with reddish hair turns slightly toward the viewer against a dark grey-green ground, painted in soft earthy tones. Cracks and small paint losses mark the edges and the background. Carel Adolph Lion Cachet painted it in 1874. The painting stayed with him. Later it belonged to his son, Dr Carel Lion Cachet of Amersfoort, who gave it to the Rijksmuseum in 1968 together with other objects.

meta: Richard Nicolaüs Roland Holst's 1888 painting of a girl from Huizen sitting under a tree beside a pond, bequeathed to the Dutch State.
about: A girl from Huizen sits under a tree beside a pond. She wears a white cap and a yellow blouse and leans against the trunk, with one arm stretched toward the sunlit grass. Sheep graze on the far side of the water, and blossoming fruit trees fill the background. The artist kept the painting until he left it to the Dutch State, together with other objects, in 1938. It reached the Rijksmuseum in 1979. Roland Holst painted it in 1888.

meta: Thomas Moran's The Juniata, Evening, bought in 1864 by George Frederick Tyler and listed as number 8 in the artist's own opus list.
about: A broad mountain valley opens under a clear blue sky, with a river winding through green fields toward distant hills. At lower left a painter works at an easel on a rocky ledge beside tall cliffs. George Frederick Tyler of Philadelphia bought the painting in 1864 and may have commissioned it. Thomas Moran recorded it as number 8 in his opus list. OP.8 is inscribed beside his signature. By 1938 it was being sold as Western Landscape. The National Gallery of Art purchased it in 2010.
credit_line: Gift of Max and Heidi Berry and Ann and Mark Kington/The Kington Foundation

meta: Jean-Baptiste Greuze's portrait of Ange Laurent de La Live de Jully, a collector who sits playing a harp.
about: A seated man in a white satin coat and pink breeches plays a harp and looks toward the viewer. At the right stand a gilded cabinet with a blue cushion and a classical draped figure in sculpture. The sitter, Ange Laurent de La Live de Jully, probably owned the picture in 1759. It then went down through his daughter's line to the Montesquiou-Fezensac family. The dealer Duveen bought it in 1937. The Kress Foundation acquired it.
